posts.text:
Applied Optoelectronics $AAOI just locked in a second hyperscaler, and the 2027 piece alone is about two-thirds of what the Street expects AOI to sell next year.

AOI signed a multiyear agreement with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer running from December 2026 through December 2030. The customer committed to buy about $1.5B of 800G transceivers in 2027 and about $0.7B of laser diodes in 2028 and 2029, so $2.2B in minimum commitments. For scale, AOI's total 2027 revenue is at $2.26B market consensus. AOI is covering a $2M one-time expense to speed up qualification, and the customer put in no capital.

The bigger number comes with an asterisk. "While not guaranteed, the current level of demand based on long-term discussions with the customer exceeds $10 billion over the four years of the LTA," said CFO Stefan Murry. Anything beyond the $2.2B depends on AOI bringing capacity online and winning more purchase commitments.

The detail I like most: AOI expects some of those laser diodes to power co-packaged optics starting in 2028, and it plans to expand laser manufacturing in Texas. It also committed to ship an agreed amount of product made in the USA starting in Q1 2027 and ramping through the year.

Why it matters: optics is one of the tightest parts of the AI buildout, and hyperscalers are now locking in multi-year supply the way they have for memory. AOI's problem has been capacity, with power delaying part of its US expansion and two ATM programs totaling $1.15B since August. This deal gives that capital a clear home, but execution on capacity is now the whole story.

posts.name: Jonkoo Capital
posts.text:
$TSM is my highest-conviction holding into 2027 here's why.

1. I don't have to pick the AI winner.

Nvidia's GPUs and the custom chips from Broadcom, Google and Amazon are mostly built at TSMC. Every debate about GPUs versus custom silicon, or which lab ends up on top, is a debate about TSMC's customers. Share moving between them matters far less to TSMC than the total being spent. High-performance computing is now 68% of revenue.

2. The growth is accelerating at a scale that shouldn't allow it.

Q3 revenue grew 50.9% year on year. October revenue grew 59.7%. Management raised its 2026 growth forecast to about 44% in dollars, from "slightly over 40%" in July. This is a company that will do well over $150bn of revenue this year.

3. The margins tell you about the competition.

Gross margin was 66.4% and operating margin 58.7% last quarter, while absorbing the start-up cost of 2nm and of new fabs in Arizona, Japan and Germany. Press reports point to another round of wafer price increases in 2027, which TSMC has not confirmed. A company that can raise prices on Nvidia and Apple does not have a real competitor at the leading edge.

4. The next leg is already in production.

2nm went from nothing to 8% of wafer revenue in three quarters, and capacity is set to more than double in 2027. New nodes dilute margins first and add to them later. That pattern played out at 5nm and 3nm, and I expect it again.

5. It pays for its own growth.

$60-64bn of capex this year and still about $90bn of net cash. The dividend was just raised 29%. In a market where the AI build-out increasingly runs on borrowed money, TSMC isn't waiting on a lender. If credit tightens for the weaker builders, the company that makes the chips for the stronger ones is where I want to be.

6. The price is not demanding.

Roughly 17x next year's earnings for a business growing earnings more than 40% this year. I don't need a higher multiple for this to work. I need the earnings to arrive.

What could break it:

I would change my mind if 2027 growth guidance came in below about 15%, if gross margin fell under 60% for reasons other than currency, or if a major customer moved a flagship chip to another foundry. None of those has happened.

Highest conviction is not the same as no risk. It means this is the position where I understand the risks best and am paid most for taking them.

AMD $AMD just got its first Helios rack running inside a Microsoft Azure lab, and the stock still broke below $400.

AMD says Microsoft accepted delivery this fall, powered up its first Helios rackscale system, and reports it is successfully running early workloads in validation. Azure plans to deploy Helios at scale and is expected to be among the first clouds to put it to work on AI inference. Per Microsoft, each liquid-cooled rack packs 72 MI455X GPUs, 18 EPYC "Venice" CPUs and 31 TB of HBM4.

Why it matters: Helios is AMD's answer to Nvidia's rack scale systems, and a hyperscaler running real workloads on it is the proof point the second half ramp needs. But this is a lab, not a customer deployment. No rack counts or financial terms were shared.

The tape did not care. AMD traded as low as $396 Tuesday, its first time under $400 since May and roughly 40% below its $649.42 high on Oct. 6, as the whole AI basket gave back Monday's Nvidia rally. Meta $META's Muse AI agent can now shop Walmart's Black Friday deals and check out for you, and it is a real test of agents with a spending limit.

Per Walmart's instructions for Muse as reported by The Verge, you tell Muse what you need, sign in to Walmart, and the first time you add an item you set up an Agent Profile with a spending limit. Then you check out inside the Muse conversation with a card saved in your Walmart account, at the same prices as http://Walmart.com. The rollout runs through Walmart's Agent Gateway and its Sparky assistant, and Walmart says Muse is just the start, with other agents on the way.

The guardrails come from Walmart's Oct. 21 announcement, which is confirmed: each agent gets its own profile, customers can require approval on every purchase or allow purchases within a limit such as $50, $100 or $200, and Walmart says agents see the same prices a human would.

Why it matters: Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents, while Walmart is opening the door on its own terms. For Meta, Muse gets a path from chat to checkout at the biggest retailer in the country right as holiday spending peaks. For the AI compute story, every agent that books, compares and buys is inference demand that never shows up in a clickstream.

Caveat: launch details are as reported. The start date moved between Nov. 23 and Nov. 24 in Walmart's own messages to The Verge, and no usage, revenue share or Meta commentary has been disclosed.

http://www.atlaspeakresearch.com/earnings/dy/2027-q3/

$DY KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM DYCOM INDUSTRIES’ FISCAL Q3 2027 EARNINGS CALL

Dycom’s November 24 call points to a divergence within infrastructure spending, not a broad investment downturn. Residential fiber construction is slowing earlier than expected as financially constrained overbuilders retreat and larger operators reassess deployment schedules. At the same time, long-haul connectivity, data-center interconnect, electrical construction, and structured cabling continue to expand. The most differentiated implications are positive for incumbent cable operators facing fewer new fiber competitors, positive for suppliers exposed to AI-network infrastructure, and negative for businesses dependent on incremental residential fiber deployments. Dycom’s cash-flow disappointment should also be separated from the strength of its data-center demand: customer credit quality, payment terms, and working-capital management are becoming more important differentiators across contractors. The assessments below distinguish high-conviction operating transmission mechanisms from uncertain earnings magnitudes. Dycom’s fiscal 2028 outlook applies predominantly to calendar 2027.

CABLE OPERATORS: SLOWER FIBER OVERBUILDING IMPROVES THE COMPETITIVE OUTLOOK (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Charter Communications (CHTR: United States) and Comcast Corporation (CMCSA: United States). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: Potentially material for Charter’s medium-term broadband earnings trajectory; moderate for Comcast at the consolidated level, given its broader business mix.

The critical evidence is management’s explanation that the fiber slowdown reflects reduced competitive urgency rather than simply construction bottlenecks. Peyovich stated, “In many cases the overbuilders have stopped,” and, “What’s really changed is just the competitive pressure.” Dycom expects fiber-to-the-home revenue to decline in fiscal 2028 despite approximately 50% growth through Q3 this year. Management also emphasized that the slowdown arrived earlier than anticipated.

The transmission mechanism favors incumbent cable networks. Fewer newly constructed fiber passings mean fewer households encounter a new competing high-speed network. That reduces the incremental pool of customers exposed to fiber introductory offers, switching campaigns, and converged mobile-broadband bundles. It can moderate churn, reduce retention spending, and preserve revenue on cable infrastructure whose fixed costs are already largely established. The benefit does not require cable to win back customers already lost to fiber; slower erosion of the existing base is economically valuable.

Charter is particularly sensitive because broadband is central to its earnings and its enlarged post-Cox footprint increases the absolute customer base exposed to competitive deployment decisions. Its November 6 results reported 233,000 pro forma Internet customer losses during Q3, including 156,000 at legacy Charter and 77,000 at legacy Cox. Comcast reported 144,000 domestic residential broadband losses in Q3. These figures establish that competitive pressure remains substantial. Dycom’s commentary supports a less adverse future competitive environment, not a claim that customer trends have already stabilized.

The near-term trading catalyst is confirmation in operators’ calendar 2027 construction budgets and commentary on competitive intensity. The operating benefit should emerge over subsequent quarters as fewer competing networks become commercially available. Existing fiber networks will continue marketing aggressively, and fixed wireless remains a separate competitive threat. Consequently, this is a positive change in the rate of competitive deterioration, not evidence that cable’s structural challenges have disappeared.

The cross-portfolio implication is important: weaker fiber-construction spending can be negative for contractors and access-equipment vendo

posts.text:
Peter Lynch said to know what you own and why you own it. Easy advice when $NVDA is ripping. A hell of a lot harder on a Friday at $125 when you don’t know if Jensen is coming back.

I bought my first shares in 2016. I’ve spent a decade studying this company, from the data center floor all the way up to the Nemotron models. I held. I added on the dips. But these last two weeks forced me to answer the same question CNBC asked me on air: What happens to NVIDIA without Jensen?

My answer was pretty blunt. He’s the lifeblood of this company. Customers plan multibillion-dollar data centers around the roadmap he lays out. Engineers who’ve spent their careers working for him have to deliver on it. If you think you can swap out the guy who built those relationships over 33 years and leave every assumption in your spreadsheet untouched, good luck with that.

So yes, if Jensen was out for good, the investment story changed for me. That’s why I pushed the Stand With Jensen petition, went on CNBC and wrote directly to NVIDIA’s board members. I wanted him back, and I told them exactly why.

Then I watched him walk back into NVIDIA. His employees were cheering. He thanked them for a second chance and told them he’d be a better CEO the second time around. After 33 years, the guy still thinks he can get better. That’s the Jensen I bet on.

Last week I was on CNBC being asked what NVIDIA looks like without him. Next week I’ll be at GTC DC hearing from Jensen himself about what he’s building next.

I fought for his comeback. Here we are. See you in DC, Jensen.

$ADI KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM ANALOG DEVICES’ Q4 FISCAL 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Analog Devices’ results support a differentiated conclusion for the broader market: demand remains strong across AI infrastructure, semiconductor test, and recovering industrial applications, but the benefits are increasingly constrained by supply availability, investment requirements, and customer-specific content exposure. The communications revenue miss was concentrated in wireless, not data center, making indiscriminate weakness in optical and AI-power suppliers difficult to justify fundamentally. Conversely, record semiconductor margins should not be equated with accelerating free cash flow, and strong component demand should not be extrapolated into stronger vehicle production or a broad telecom capital-spending recovery. The highest-conviction implications favor suppliers addressing physical bottlenecks and manufacturers with available capacity, while highlighting weaker earnings conversion at capacity builders and cost pressure in slower-growing equipment markets. Magnitude assessments below describe business sensitivity, not predicted share-price movements. Country labels identify the listing market of the ticker shown.

OPTICAL NETWORKING: THE COMMUNICATIONS MISS WAS NOT AN AI DEMAND MISS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Coherent (COHR: US) and Lumentum Holdings (LITE: US). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high relevance to their data-center businesses and material relevance to consolidated growth; the incremental earnings uplift attributable specifically to ADI’s disclosure cannot be quantified.

ADI’s communications revenue of approximately $707 million missed the $725 million consensus estimate, but management explicitly attributed the shortfall to wireless. Data center represented 83% of communications revenue, grew more than 100% year-over-year, and increased slightly more than 10% sequentially. Management further stated, “Optical did grow a bit faster than power.” The important distinction is that a disappointing aggregate communications result concealed continued strength in the economically larger AI infrastructure business.

The transmission mechanism is increased deployment of high-bandwidth optical connections combined with more demanding laser control, tuning, monitoring, and power requirements. ADI participates in the control functions surrounding optical systems; Coherent and Lumentum supply complementary photonic components, modules, and optical subsystems. Greater optical complexity can therefore support demand across several parts of the same architecture without requiring identical supplier growth rates.

This interpretation is corroborated by already-published peer results. Coherent’s 11/04/26 release described the transition from copper to optical connectivity as a growth driver and projected fiscal 2027 pro forma revenue growth exceeding 60%. Lumentum’s 11/02/26 release identified optical circuit switches among its leading growth contributors and disclosed another major near-package/co-packaged optics win supported by purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion. ADI’s call provides additional corroboration, not a new award to either company.

Near-term significance centers on the 11/24 semiconductor selloff and subsequent differentiation between wireless weakness and optical strength. The longer-duration benefit is higher optical content as bandwidth and architectural complexity increase. ADI’s results do not establish that every optical implementation benefits equally, nor do they identify supplier allocations within particular hyperscaler systems. They nevertheless provide strong evidence against treating the communications miss as an early warning of weakening AI optical demand.

POWER SEMICONDUCTORS: CONTENT GROWTH IS BROADENING, BUT PROFITS WILL NOT BE UNCONTESTED (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected companies: Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR: US) and Infineon Technologies

posts.name: Mark Minervini
posts.text:
Yesterday’s rally may have looked impressive, with a huge number of stocks up 10%, 20%, even 30%. But when you put those moves into perspective, it’s clear the market still has work to do.
$QQQ recovered only a relatively small portion of its recent decline and remains below a declining 10-day moving average. Most of the AI/Tech names look similar - big percentage rallies, but still badly damaged charts in well-established downtrends. 
Volume on both the Nasdaq and NYSE was below the previous day. Nvidia reinstating its founder appeared to be the catalyst that ignited the rally, but the market was already heavily oversold and poised for a bounce. One day and one man are not enough to change the trend.
So the question is whether the major indexes have established a low or yesterday was simply a sharp oversold rally within an ongoing correction. Historically, some of the biggest rallies occur during bear markets.
Even if the major indexes fail to reach bear market correction percentage declines, a bear market in tech has already occurred. There are far too many stocks down 50-80%, to dismiss the declines as healthy pullbacks.
What happens from here is what matters. We need to see follow-through buying, broader participation and improving breadth. More importantly, before getting aggressive, I want to see quality stocks setting up and breaking out of sound bases - not simply broken leaders bouncing back into well-established downtrends.
Interest rates remain an obstacle. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed that policymakers remain concerned about inflation and that additional tightening may still be necessary.
On the positive side, we’re entering what has historically been a favorable November-December period, and the months following midterm elections have also tended to be strong, particularly during the first half of the following year.
One could argue whether those historical tailwinds will be strong enough to overcome a rising-rate environment. But I should also point out that we would never allow seasonality, cycle work - or the Fed, for that matter - to override what the market itself is actually telling us.
Those are all factors to consider, but in my world, price and volume, breadth, leadership and the action of individual stocks ultimately have the final say. 
For now, the market still has to prove itself. http://minervini.com

posts.text:
Yesterday, the President of the United States said he personally convinced the board of the world's most valuable company to reinstate its CEO. $NVDA

Nvidia's own statement says the board acted after receiving "input from senior levels of the United States government."

Whatever you think of Jensen Huang, and I think he is one of the great business builders of our time, this should give every investor pause. A public company's board answers to its shareholders. Not to the White House.

It reminded me of a 2002 episode of The West Wing. A company called Anteras is facing collapse after a massive recall. A chip company, no less! Leo McGarry wants the government to guarantee its loans. President Bartlet, an economist, refuses:

Bartlet: "The marketplace will take care of Anteras."
Leo: "The marketplace will kill Anteras."
Bartlet: "That's what's supposed to happen."
There was a second reason. The CEO had been a huge campaign contributor. Bartlet understood that a president doing favors for a donor's company, even a defensible favor, corrodes trust in the system.

Some will say The West Wing was a liberal show. That's exactly the point. Even Aaron Sorkin's Democratic president believed the market, not the White House, should decide a company's fate. This isn't liberal versus conservative. It's about free markets.

When Washington starts picking CEOs, we should all be concerned.

Twenty-four years later, the scene seems almost quaint. Those were the days.

posts.text:
Top Republican calls Trump’s pressure on  $NVDA board to bring back Jensen a “slippery slope.”  A gift to Dems? 

McCormick Warns of ‘Slippery Slope’ After Trump Pressured Nvidia
▪Republican Senator Dave McCormick warned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp. board could create a “slippery slope.”
▪McCormick wants the Senate Banking Committee to focus on whether any laws were broken or national security was compromised to get advanced chips into the hands of China.
▪McCormick supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

By Erik Wasson and Annmarie Hordern
11/24/2026 07:35:50
(Bloomberg) -- Republican Senator Dave McCormickwarned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp. board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could create a “slippery slope.” 

“I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in really ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions,” McCormick, the former chief of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, told Bloomberg TV. “This is a precedent that I don’t think we want to replicate or reinforce.”

McCormick, who sidestepped questions about whether the Nvidia board erred in its decision to bring back Huang, will have the opportunity to question the embattled CEO next week when he testifies publicly before the Senate Banking Committee. 

The Pennsylvania senator said he wants the panel to focus its questioning on whether any laws were broken, national security was compromised or Department of Commerce rules circumvented to get advanced chips into the hands of China. 
“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” said McCormick, a former Commerce Department export control official. “I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts.”
The comments are the latest sign that members of Trump’s own party are breaking with the president on his handling of China, artificial intelligence and Nvidia’s embattled leader.
￼
Senator Dave McCormick discusses the questions he wants answered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the need to update legislation on export controls.

US lawmakers are looking to attach export control provisions to the annual defense policy bill set for votes in the House and Senate in December. McCormick’s comments echo a Monday X post by Senate Intelligence Chairman Tom Cotton, who said such provisions will be passed one way or another. 

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bill,” Cotton said. 

McCormick, when asked about Trump’s market involvement, also said he supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials. He warned that such measures will be needed to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

posts.text:
This is interesting.

Yesterday, President Trump revealed the Jensen Huang news 29 minutes before it was made public, but almost no one realized, on Monday at 8:29 AM ET.

Timeline of events:

- Sunday, 10:40 AM ET: Treasury Secretary Bessent reverses review and says door is open for Jensen's return

- Sunday, 3:36 PM ET: We post that "something is happening behind the scenes" at Nvidia, $NVDA

- Sunday 9:54 PM ET: President Trump says he "hopes" Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO (we now know Trump already knew he would be reinstated at this point)

- Monday, 8:29 AM ET: President Trump tells PBS News reporter that Jensen is "back where he should be" then quickly says "I don't want to comment anymore"

- Monday, 8:58 AM ET: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO, and Board Director

- Monday, 9:07 AM ET: President Trump releases a statement saying Nvidia has made the "correct and proper decision"

- Monday, 9:25 AM ET: President Trump tells CNBC he personally joined an Nvidia board meeting over the weekend to help reinstate Jensen Huang

President Trump then confirms he knew about the reinstatement at least a day prior to the announcement.

Following the right people on X is the ultimate source of alpha.

posts.text: $A  Agilent beat and the market noticed. Fourth-quarter revenue $2.04 billion, up 9.6%, EPS $1.59, and the stock is up 7.3% premarket. In a tape where beats get sold, a clean print with growth still moves. Agilent is not an AI name and not a headline name. It is a tools company with a quarter that grew, and on a morning when the leaders give back, the quiet beat is the one that holds. That is the split in this market: the names that need a story fall on the story, and the names with a number hold on the number. Watch whether Agilent keeps the gain into the close. A premarket pop is a claim. A close above the open is a hold.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text: $HPE reported after the close and fell 9.6% premarket anyway. Fourth-quarter revenue $14.5 billion, up 50%, EPS $1.26, and the stock gave it all back after rising more than 17% on Monday. That is the pattern of this earnings season. The number is not the problem and the price is. Earnings season does not reward the quarter anymore. It rewards the guide, the cash, and the slope of what is already contracted, and it punishes anything that leaves a question open. $HPE had the revenue. The market wanted the next part. Watch whether the stock holds its Monday gain into the close, because a print that falls 10% premarket is the market saying the bar was higher than the number.

$SMTC KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM SEMTECH’S Q3 FISCAL 2027 EARNINGS CALL

Semtech’s results strengthen the demand outlook for AI connectivity, but the more consequential cross-market implication is a redistribution of semiconductor content within that growing market. Data center revenue increased 45% sequentially to $145 million, with approximately $203 million implied for Q4 and management expecting more than $1 billion in fiscal 2028. Simultaneously, a new hyperscaler design win demonstrated that linear equalizers can replace retimers in selected applications, while NPO adoption creates additional opportunities for analog electronics, lasers, and optical packaging. These developments favor qualified optical manufacturing capacity and differentiated physical-layer components, while challenging assumptions of universally rising DSP and retimer content. Outside AI infrastructure, LoRa provides a selective positive signal for industrial connectivity, whereas memory constraints remain a negative for handset production. The implications below distinguish product-level effects from consolidated earnings effects; country labels identify operational headquarters rather than legal incorporation.

HIGH-SPEED COPPER AND RETIMERS

LINEAR EQUALIZERS CREATE A CREDIBLE COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE TO RETIMER ATTACH RATES (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Credo Technology Group (CRDO: United States). Direction: negative for the longer-term opportunity in overlapping Ethernet retimers and short-reach active electrical cables. Magnitude: potentially material within contested applications, but insufficient evidence for a near-term consolidated earnings reduction.

The key disclosure was not simply another active copper cable win. Semtech secured an onboard linear equalizer design win at a 2nd hyperscaler for a major inference platform, with deployment expected in the first half of fiscal 2028, approximately February through July 2027. Management said the solution achieved signal integrity “on par with an onboard retimer,” while “reducing power consumption by 90% and eliminating added latency.” Separately, the initial hyperscaler awarded Semtech 2 additional ACC platform wins.

The transmission mechanism is a reduction in retimer attachment where channel conditions permit a lower-power analog implementation. Credo sells Ethernet retimers and AECs, so successful qualification of linear alternatives creates a competing route to solving some of the same signal-integrity problems. Customers gain an alternative that can reduce component power, latency, and potentially system cost. Even without immediate displacement, credible alternatives can constrain future pricing and reduce the proportion of high-speed links that investors should assume require full retiming.

The distinction between applications is critical. The new onboard win is not evidence that Credo lost an AEC socket, and Semtech did not identify the displaced supplier. Semtech described production ACC reach of approximately 2.5 meters at 1.6T, while Credo has described an AEC opportunity spanning approximately 1 to 7 meters. The overlap is therefore partial. Retimers retain advantages in regeneration, reach, diagnostics, and difficult channel conditions. This evidence also should not be extrapolated automatically to PCIe retimers.

The near-term trading catalyst is Credo’s December 1, 2026 earnings call, particularly commentary on 1.6T adoption, Ethernet retimer attachment, and competition at large customers. The fundamental impact belongs mainly to calendar 2027 and subsequent platform generations, rather than the already-completed October quarter. Credo’s expanding optical transceiver, DSP, silicon-photonics, and interconnect portfolio provides substantial offsets. The actionable negative is to the assumption of protected retimer and AEC economics across every short-reach link, not to aggregate connectivity demand or Credo’s entire business

I heavily disagree with your other comment when you say Jensen doesn't solve anything. 

Jensen doesn't change macro issues with interest rates, credit/cash tightening (aside from maybe supplier financing).

People argue downside reflexivity today:
-> valuations crash
-> less willingness to support vendor financing/guarantees. 
-> outflow to other ecosystems like TPUs + $AMD (Nvidia ecosystem push decline further eg. CPO), and so on. 
-> cycle of suck

Then there's other concurrent issues like the $500B AI financing with insurance + residual guarantees that was in trouble with Jensen gone. 

But same can be applied the other way upstream again with valuations + confidence + financing with Jensen's return. 

This is different from saying there's going to be a cash crunch and aggregate AI capex will keep exponentially increasing, my point is very narrow. 

But I'd argue Jensen alone does meaningfully increase upstream AI capex spend than when he's gone.

Ray Dalio says investors mistake great technology for a great investment in a bubble and compares the AI boom with the innovations of the 1920s

“A lot of people think a bubble is whether the price gets beyond that which can come from the present value of future cash flows, and that’s not it, because what happens is you don’t know the future cash flows for decades, let’s say, if you take the present value.

“In any case, even those with good financial cash flows have had bubbles. So you could see the 1920s bubbles, and then you have the collapses. Even if they work out in the long run, you have the bubble bursting.

“The bubble, the mechanics of it, is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment.

“In the ’20s, imagine what that was like. That was the first time you had electricity in houses, so you had lighting and you had refrigeration. You had movies, you had radio, you had cars, you had airplanes—all of this new technology coming on. It would be more apparent than anything we’ve seen even with AI.”

posts.name: Jerry Capital
posts.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 is starting to look less like science fiction and more like an extreme extrapolation of modern America.

The central premise of cyberpunk is "high tech, low life": extraordinary technological advancement without a corresponding improvement in everyone's quality of life.

Consider the parallels:

- Arasaka and Militech: Technology and defense giants becoming increasingly intertwined with government and national security.

- Corporate political power: Billionaires increasingly influencing elections, government policy and regulation.

- Corporate surveillance: AI-powered monitoring, facial recognition and commercial data brokers.

- Trauma Team: A healthcare system where access and quality are heavily influenced by personal wealth.*

- Cybernetic augmentation: Neuralink, brain-computer interfaces and advanced prosthetics.

- Rogue AI and the Blackwall: Autonomous AI agents, cybersecurity threats and increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

- Corporate-controlled infrastructure: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and SpaceX controlling critical technological infrastructure.

- Extreme class divisions: Concentrated asset ownership, deteriorating housing affordability and enormous disparities in wealth.

- Digital escapism: AI companions, immersive virtual worlds and algorithmically addictive entertainment.

America is obviously nowhere near Night City in terms of violence, institutional collapse or corporate sovereignty. Democratic institutions and legal protections still constrain corporate power.

But the underlying trajectory is remarkably similar: technological abundance alongside economic insecurity, increasingly powerful corporations alongside governments dependent on their capabilities, and extraordinary private wealth alongside persistent social problems.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Cyberpunk 2077 is that it depicts a future in which capitalism and technological innovation succeed spectacularly, but society fails to distribute their benefits broadly.

Technological progress does not automatically translate into social progress.

*The trauma team intro is the best part of the game?

Gavin Baker warns Huawei hardware might now get better really fast, so the new China chip policies carry enormous risks for American national security

"And I've been with Jensen all over the world, many situations. The only thing I've ever heard him say about China is the absolute importance of America beating China. And the only thing I've ever heard him say about Chinese hardware is the absolute importance of making sure that American AI hardware dominates."

"And we do not let an alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem develop because that AI ecosystem could be given to our real adversaries, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and China's been working hard on this. But the policies that Jensen was advocating for, I think, were essentially guaranteed to keep America in the lead in AI for the foreseeable future."
"Now, we're going to do new policies. And I think those policies carry enormous risks for American national security because I think the odds that China, who is a formidable competitor, now that they are forced to develop their own ecosystem, it's not an option."

"Before, the Chinese government was trying to encourage Huawei, ironically restricting the imports of GPUs. But Nvidia GPUs, less powerful than available in America, Jensen said America should have the first, the best, and the most, were available in China and the labs preferred those. That was slowing down Huawei because to make the hardware better, it needs to be used. Now that Huawei hardware is going to be used by every Chinese AI lab, I think it might get better really fast."

quoted.text:
The most important line:

“Right now, DeepSeek is paying the price for reliability, while domestic chips are *learning* how to recover from cluster failures at their expense.”

Learning is the important word and Huawei is now going to learn at a much faster rate.

Our old policy was guaranteed to always keep America ahead while maximizing our leverage, while the new policy is super risky, might eliminate our leverage in a few short years and could result in super power-inefficient but computationally sufficient Huawei clusters appearing in Iran, Russia and North Korea.

Steven Bartlett: “What are you investing in in this moment? I’ve been thinking a lot about this.”

Steve Eisman: “Let’s say I own 100 shares of Nvidia, just make up a number, and I’ve owned it for a very long time. And I’m nervous. The problem is, if I sell my Nvidia, I’ve got to pay massive taxes on the gain. And I don’t want to do that, unless I’m so freaked out that I’ll do it anyway. You’re talking about 30%, 35% taxes. “So what you can do for a time, you can’t do it forever, is I can short 50 shares or 75 shares or even 100 shares of Nvidia. So now my Nvidia exposure is a lot lower.

“If I were to do that today, I’d have to cover the entire position at the end of January. That’s just the way the tax rules work. But during that period, I wouldn’t have any real exposure to Nvidia. That’s what I did.”

Steve Jobs sold 6.5 million shares of Apple in 1985 after getting forced out of the company he co founded, keeping only 1 share so he could still read the annual reports

Had he kept that stake, it would have been worth an estimated $66 billion by 2016

Months after his ouster, Jobs bought a struggling computer graphics unit from George Lucas for $10 million and named it Pixar

He burned through roughly $50 million of his own cash keeping Pixar alive for nearly a decade until Toy Story turned into a $180 million domestic hit, and in 2006 he sold the studio to Disney for $7.4 billion

Right before Apple bought his other company NeXT and brought him back in 1997 with 90 days of cash left, Jobs went on television and tore into Apple's leadership for standing still despite spending billions on research

Once he took back control, Jobs set his salary at $1 a year for 15 years, while Apple gifted him a $90 million Gulfstream V private jet and stock awards that grew his holdings to $2.2 billion

In the 1996 interview below, filmed just months before his return, Jobs brags about Pixar's $180 million box office run and diagnoses why Apple became one of Wall Street's biggest failures

posts.name: TheValueist
posts.text:
October 28 results independently showed organic orders increasing more than 100% and organic revenue increasing 55%. HPE therefore provides customer-side corroboration of the infrastructure bottleneck, not the first evidence of the cycle. This distinction reduces the justification for treating the call as a standalone near-term earnings upgrade.

The timing implication is more nuanced than simply moving every supplier forecast into HPE’s second half. Some power and cooling equipment must be delivered before IT systems are installed; commissioning can occur later. HPE’s schedule confirms dependency on facility completion but does not establish Vertiv’s project-specific order or revenue dates.

Near-term catalyst: Backlog conversion, installation progress, commissioning, and customer site-readiness disclosures are more actionable than aggregate AI-order announcements. Delayed facilities can defer IT revenue even when underlying demand remains intact.

Longer-duration implication: Rising rack density and more complex liquid-cooled infrastructure support higher engineering and service requirements. However, liquid cooling transfers heat rather than eliminating it, and specific chiller, heat-exchanger, or fluid-distribution content depends on architecture. The high-conviction read-through is sustained demand for critical infrastructure, not an undisclosed HPE design win or a universal increase in every cooling component.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
I like this and I can get behind most of it. Regime risk is real and trend is one of the best tools for it, which is why I own it. 

Where I get stuck is the core part (or sizing the asset match right, as it pertains to my framework). The T-bill collateral is great, but I can own T-bills directly, and in an ALM framework that's exactly what funds the near-term liabilities. The overlay on top is what I'm evaluating, and it has no cash flows I can use to estimate a return or match against a liability. Structurally agnostic to direction isn't the same as unconditional either. It still needs sustained trends. 

And on the sequence math, the research points to the first decade of real returns, not the first five years. That's where trend's lost-decade risk shows up. So, in an ALM framework this isn't really a debate about whether to use trend, but whether trend is a better long-term matching instrument than other long-term options (clearly better than long duration bonds, but that argument is not nearly as robust compared to equities). The long-term stuff is, as @choffstein says, a statistical bet and there's no clear winner there given past isn't indicative of future returns and all that....

So I'd frame it this way: the core is whatever I can plan around, and trend is insurance against the core's assumptions breaking. That case gets me to a bigger satellite, maybe 15%+. It doesn't get me to a foundation on its own (which is where a multi-asset "stacked" instrument probably makes a more appealing core argument). 

Again, none of this is an argument against trend (definitely not against stacking trend). It's a quibble over trend as the main asset in a portfolio when compared to something like equities where, as I recently framed it in my 50 page research piece (which, no one read as well, lol), I framed the opportunity cost as potentially gigantic in the long-run. But as you note, that's basically a bet on stable Capitalism in the future, and  I feel pretty good about that bet.

The stop loss was too tight on a very volatile name and caused me to miss a big trade

The agent now calculates its stop loss based on IV (implied volatility), a measure of how much movement the market expects. 

When markets get choppy and a contract’s IV rises, its stop can widen from 20% to 40%, giving the trade more room to move.

If the agent does increase the stop loss it will reduce the size of the trade which helps manage risk

Having the right stop loss and take profit levels is just as important as having a good strategy and this update was an important one

I discussed this idea in depth in ATG, where i share education about my trading agents and help others build their own

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. I’m usually a fan of the @davidmcw podcast, but episodes 93 and 95 on Jensen Huang and AI contained some significant inaccuracies. Three examples:

Neoclouds: The suggestion that neoclouds rent capacity from hyperscalers gets the business model backwards.
They finance and operate GPU infrastructure, then rent compute to AI companies and other customers including Microsoft.

Open models: The discussion of Jensen’s position on China and AI overlooks his strong advocacy for open models. He has explicitly argued that open and closed models will both thrive, and that open models are vital to businesses, developers and national AI ecosystems. This is central to understanding his position.

Who captures the profits? The claim that Taiwan and Korea manufacture the chips and pocket the real profits overlooks Nvidia’s economics. CUDA, GPU architecture, networking and integrated systems give Nvidia enormous pricing power and margins. It is far more than a chip designer outsourcing manufacturing.

These aren't minor technical details. They fundamentally shape how listeners understand the AI industry. You can be sceptical about AI valuations without getting the underlying economics wrong.

I hope David addresses these points and applies more rigorous fact-checking in future episodes. I’m a fan of the podcast, which is why the standard of analysis matters.

My 9 Takeaways From Jensen Huang’s Return As Nvidia’s CEO

In a wild turn of events, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia yesterday. The news will be regurgitated in every media outlet around the world, so I am only going to focus on my takeaways this morning.

First, Jensen just solidified his spot on the Mount Rushmore of technology founders. No one else could return to the company they founded three decades ago and watch the US stock market increase by $3 trillion in a matter of minutes. It was surreal watching the market surge in real-time as the news spread, but maybe we shouldn’t be surprised given Jensen is largely thought of as the godfather of the AI industry.

Second, this is a great reminder that the voice of shareholders will usually be heard. The board of directors misplayed their hand and tried to over-govern the situation. Given the immediate and severe sell-off in Nvidia’s stock price, it is clear that shareholders disagreed with the board’s decision to force Jensen to resign. Add in the ridiculous stock recovery of more than 30% upon his return and it is clear that shareholders want Jensen at the helm of the company.

Third, Jensen needs to immediately remove the entire board of directors. He can’t operate a business with board members that were willing to force him out of his company and risk trillions of dollars in shareholder value. These directors showed their true colors, which is now a risk to Nvidia. For better or worse, you need directors that are loyal to the company and shareholders, not a group of people whose opinion will blow with the wind of public sentiment.

Fourth, the AI trade is about to catch a second wind. The recent market sell-off gave everyone time to take a deep breath, but demand is still outstripping supply, so we are going much higher.

Fifth, reports have surfaced that President Trump and the White House intervened in the Nvidia saga, including participating in a board meeting to lay out their case for Jensen being reinstated. We knew the White House was more involved in the market through their investment decisions, but this is probably the first time in history that the US government had an executive reinstated. We should consider Nvidia indirectly run by the US government going forward.

Sixth, the return of Jensen Huang was widely celebrated across the internet. The only word of caution that I saw worth mentioning is that Enron’s CEO, Ken Lay, was reinstated months before the company collapsed due to accounting fraud. I have no reason to believe Nvidia is a fraud, and I have to assume the US government told Nvidia’s board the company would not be prosecuted, so this is more a fun fact than anything else.

Seventh, the mainstream media is absolutely cooked. They spent weeks writing hit pieces about Jensen’s management style, and claiming that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, but none of that mattered. The founder of the world’s most valuable company has rightfully taken his spot atop his empire once again. No one cares about the mainstream media hit pieces anymore.

Eighth, the United States and Nvidia should race to flood the Chinese market with Nvidia chips. If they don’t, the Chinese companies will start building their own chips and have a good chance of creating more superior technology over time. Chinese chips that are better than the US chips would be a nightmare for the US government, so it is better for us to keep China addicted to Nvidia’s current chips. This is a complex game that will be played out over years, but I firmly believe China’s independence on chips is a significant risk that the US can’t risk.

Lastly, it is clear that the American closed-source AI labs do not want open-source AI technology to succeed. That is the number one reason why everyone else should want open-source AI to proliferate. With this understanding, Jensen and Nvidia should sink billions of dollars into American open-source AI technology and come for the closed-source labs with a vengeance

procurement event. The high-conviction conclusion is narrower: wireless equipment has a less favorable combination of growth and input-cost pressure than AI optical infrastructure.

Near-term trading significance lies in distinguishing wireless weakness from data-center strength after ADI’s release. The fundamental test extends into 2027 as Ericsson attempts to offset component costs through pricing, portfolio actions, and efficiency. This supports relative caution toward RAN earnings quality, not a thesis of an imminent wireless demand collapse.

CROSS-PORTFOLIO RISK: MORE AI SUPPLIERS DO NOT NECESSARILY PROVIDE MORE DIVERSIFICATION (READ-THROUGH 11)

Affected companies: Analog Devices (ADI: US), Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR: US), Teradyne (TER: US), Coherent (COHR: US), Lumentum Holdings (LITE: US), and Vertiv Holdings (VRT: US). Direction: negative for diversification assumptions, despite the positive operating outlook. Magnitude: potentially high for portfolios holding several of these exposures.

ADI’s direct data-center revenue represented approximately 13% of sales, but management grouped data center, ATE, and aerospace and defense into a larger approximately 30% revenue pool benefiting from unusually strong demand. Additional AI-linked demand appears in energy, power infrastructure, and automation. Consequently, direct data-center reporting understates some companies’ economic sensitivity to the infrastructure investment cycle.

The transmission mechanism is a shared final spending driver across different supply-chain stages. Hyperscaler and accelerator-platform investment supports optical connectivity, power semiconductors, semiconductor test, and cooling infrastructure. These businesses have different products, customers, and shipment timing, but a change in deployment schedules or infrastructure budgets can propagate through several holdings simultaneously.

ADI’s statement that more than 2/3 of fiscal 2026 growth came from non-AI-centric opportunities remains an important offset. ADI is not a pure-play AI supplier, and the affected companies should not be treated as having identical sensitivities. Nevertheless, product diversification and numerous SKUs do not establish independence from the same ultimate capital-spending decisions.

The near-term risk is correlated trading during semiconductor and AI-infrastructure de-risking, even when individual earnings releases remain strong. The longer-duration risk is that supply-chain orders, inventory buffers, and capacity expansions amplify a subsequent change in final demand. The portfolio implication is to aggregate these exposures by underlying infrastructure spending and cash-flow dependence, rather than treating analog chips, optical components, test equipment, and cooling systems as fully separate risk categories.

🦔Oracle put out a statement insisting it has all the money it needs to build out its OpenAI contract, adding that “any media reports that will come out and say the contrary are incorrect and wrong,” about reports that hadn’t even come out yet.

My Take
Oracle denied the news before it existed, which is a strange move for a company that says everything’s fine. Part of its “fully funded” plan is vendor financing, meaning the companies selling it the equipment are also lending it the money to pay for that equipment. Oracle also admits free cash flow won’t turn positive until the second half of fiscal 2028.

So Oracle burns cash for another year or more on its suppliers’ credit, and the rent checks that make it all work come from OpenAI, which lost about $11.5 billion in a single quarter. If OpenAI slows down, Oracle ends up owning a lot of very expensive buildings with one big tenant who can’t pay.

Hedgie🤗

In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the  process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history.

You can read the full post here:

https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.

With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found.

I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history.

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. Colette Kress, qui assurait l'intérim, reste CFO et Harvey Jones reste chairman. Côté garde-fous, l'enquête interne continue, un comité sécurité nationale et contrôle export est mis en place et Nvidia cherche un chief compliance officer.

B/ La demande était intacte dans les chiffres, le marché rend la décote de gouvernance. Par contre, ça expose un énorme key-man risk chez Nvidia, il n'y a juste pas de plan B. Et les shorts restent encore gagnants de 14 Md$ depuis fin octobre, ils ont largement du gras pour revenir à la charge

C'est l'une des meilleur sessions de l'histoire de Wall-Street pour la tech. Lunaire après la semaine horrible

2. Ce que son retour change vraiment

Au-delà du rebond immédiat, c'est un signal fort pour tout l'écosystème IA. Le retour de Jensen redonne à Nvidia sa capacité à fédérer l'industrie, sécurise sa culture interne et rassure sur l'exécution de la roadmap produit déjà annoncée, ce qui ouvre la porte à un re-rating du multiple.   

Deux zones grises restent quand même sur la table. D'abord, rien ne garantit que Nvidia pourra continuer à monter des gros investissements multi-parties avec ses partenaires de l'écosystème à la même échelle qu'avant. Ensuite, le réglementaire reste un vrai poids

Needless to say, this move comes at a challenging time for academia.

Rapid AI advances are fundamentally reshaping how knowledge is created, disseminated, and applied. Universities must rethink their roles in a world where frontier AI systems can perform tasks once requiring years of specialized training. 1965 – Her şey küçük bir fikirle başladı.
İsveç'in Malmö kentinde yaşayan ahşap ustası Henning Eklund, diş aralarını temizlemek için yeni bir ürün geliştirmek istedi. 

TePe marka Diş Fırçalarını hiç duydunuz mu?
TePe'nin hikayesi bir marangozdan küresel markaya uzanıyor.

Malmö Diş Hekimliği Fakültesi'ndeki profesörlerle iş birliği yaptı ve diş aralarının doğal anatomisine uyum sağlayan üçgen biçimli ahşap kürdan geliştirdi.

TePe böyle doğdu.
1973 – Diş fırçası üretimine geçiş
Henning'in oğlu Bertil Eklund işi devraldı ve şirketin ürün yelpazesini genişletti. 1973 yılında ilk TePe diş fırçası üretildi. Marka zamanla İsveç'te ciddi bir pazar payına ulaştı. Şirketin kendi tarihçesine göre İsveç'te satın alınan diş fırçalarının dörtte birinden fazlası TePe markalı hale geldi.

1993 – Asıl büyüme motoru ortaya çıktı.
Şirket 1993 yılında diş arası fırçalarını piyasaya sürdü.
Bu ürün grubu TePe'nin en önemli büyüme alanlarından biri oldu. Çünkü şirket yalnızca diş fırçası satmak yerine, insanların çoğunlukla ihmal ettiği diş arası temizliğine odaklanan bir uzmanlık geliştirmişti.

1997–2012  Uluslararası marka olma dönemi
CEO Birgitta Nilsson döneminde ihracata ve yurt dışı yapılanmasına ağırlık verildi. Şirketin cirosu yaklaşık 30 milyon İsveç kronundan 300 milyon İsveç kronuna yükseldi.

2012 yılında kurucunun torunu Joel Eklund CEO oldu ve uluslararası büyümeyi sürdürdü. 

Şirket 1965'te çok küçük ve spesifik bir probleme odaklandı. Diş aralarının temizliği. Sonra bu alanda uzmanlaştı, diş hekimleriyle iş birliği yaptı, ürün gamını genişletti ve küresel bir marka oluşturdu.

Yani önce bir ihtiyacı keşfetti, sonra o ihtiyacın uzmanı oldu. 

Bu markanın farklı ürünleri şu anda indirimde. 200-500 TL civarı.

posts.name: Jonesy
posts.text:
NVDA +31% Monday, its third best day ever, after the board reinstated Jensen Huang 11 days after he resigned. The stock had lost about a third of its value in that window, roughly $1.7T of market cap. Even after Monday it’s still around 12% below where it was on Nov 12.

The CEO question got settled. These didn’t:

1.Investigations
• SEC enforcement is examining Nvidia’s accounting
• DOJ antitrust is reviewing the $12.9B Hugging Face deal, plus whether customers got bigger GPU allocations if they also bought Nvidia networking and Groq chips
• DOJ is also looking at whether the Groq license and hiring deal was set up to avoid antitrust review
• The California AG served an investigative subpoena on Nov 19
• Commerce added Megaspeed, the Singapore partner Alice Huang used to run, to the trade blacklist on Nov 23
• The board’s own investigation is still open, and Nvidia is searching for a new chief compliance officer

2.Geographic disclosure
Nvidia switched revenue reporting from billing address to customer HQ, and Singapore dropped out of the breakdown. Per the FT, that happened as Singapore sales were nearing half of global revenue.

3.Circular financing
• ~$50B invested in model makers (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), with total ecosystem equity stakes about double that
• $30B into OpenAI in February
• Up to $105B of lease guarantees on the Ohio campus where OpenAI is the tenant
• Up to $6.3B of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity committed through 2032
• $3.5B in guarantees on cloud partners’ data center leases, against $712M in escrow
• BNEF puts Nvidia’s direct credit support at $198B+
On the Nov 17 call, Kress said Nvidia will be “far more selective” on financing deals going forward.

4.Debt load
• AI computing debt issuance: $680B through October vs $130B in all of 2023
• About 31% of nonfinancial IG issuance, up from under 6% in 2023
• $1.1T+ outstanding, and the largest banks have close to $1T of exposure
• On-balance-sheet debt at the seven largest AI firms is expected to top $800B by year end
• Another $3T+ in leases that haven’t started yet, take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees that aren’t counted as debt

http://5.Credit stress
• HSBC sold $300M of Stargate Project Jupiter construction debt at under 90 cents after Oracle sent a force majeure notice
• ING is trying to find buyers for $500M of data center loans
• Data center CDS are at record highs, and some project bonds yield double digits
• IG bonds backed by data centers trade about 146bps wider than the tenants’ own debt

6.Duration mismatch
Loans of 10 to 40 years are being written against GPUs with a 2 to 3 year economic life. Moody’s says the contracts backing CoreWeave’s $2.6B DDTL average about 3.1 years.

7.Washington
Democrats take both chambers in January. Huang and GC Tim Teter have transcribed House interviews Dec 1-2, and Huang has a public Senate Banking hearing Dec 3.

The CEO risk got repriced in one session. The credit, accounting and regulatory risks didn’t

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
OpenAI's Noam Brown predicts AI progress will keep accelerating and says his most controversial take is that promising students should drop out and join the labs now

"The way the technology is developing, I think we're lucky that it is jagged and that there are things that the models are quite bad at. But in the same way that these models can now do superhuman math research, I do think there is a case that even if they are spiky and jagged, they can be directed towards being really good at RSI. And in that case, you might see very rapid progress."

"Now, I still think you get bottlenecked on certain things. I think you get bottlenecked by compute. I think you get bottlenecked by the long tail of things that the models are bad at and humans are necessary for. But I do think that things go much faster."

"We have seen a lot of rapid progress over the past few years when it comes to AI. I think even in the past six months that progress has, if anything, accelerated. And I think that we're going to continue to see a very steep rate of progress over the next year or two."

"Perhaps my most controversial take is that if somebody is a promising student, the best thing to do is actually to drop out and join the labs now."

quoted.text:
OpenAI's Noam Brown says an AI that can read faces would have a 20% chance to win the World Series of Poker within five years

LIN: "Within the next five years, if AI is allowed to play in the World Series of Poker, do you think AI will beat all the humans?"

BROWN: "One AI?"

LIN: "One AI agent. Not all AI. One AI agent. There's a lot of variance in the game."

BROWN: "This is a great question because if it is playing GTO, no, because I think the variance is too high in the game. That said, I could see a case that if the AI is superhuman at reading people, if it's able to read people's faces and basically detect whether they're bluffing or not, I could see it being extremely superhuman at that and basically being able to read the other person's cards."

"And in that case, even then, it's probably not a high probability that it wins because there's still a luck factor, right? You can just go all in preflop every single hand and then just leave it to the luck of the draw. But I would give it a good 20% chance that it could win."

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
Ben Thompson argues that unlike Sam Altman, Jensen Huang was targeted by "a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors"

"That said, I didn't think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech: whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company's investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act."

"And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I've invoked the phrase "Show me the man and I'll show you the crime" over the past few weeks, but it's worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, "Which one?", at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned."

quoted.text:
Ben Thompson argues the chip ban is an 'insane policy' that will destroy America’s chip industry in the long run, because it gives China the imperative to build its own

“The chip ban is a fairly insane policy that flies in the face of how the US has managed technology transfer for the last fifty years. It’s the people who are doing the chip ban who should be explaining why suddenly this is a good idea.”

“The chip ban is the foundation of destroying our chip industry in the long run, because you are creating the incentives for the demand.”

“This has always been the issue with the whole China stuff. You’re like, oh, China knows they need to make chips, they’re gonna make chips. You don’t just make chips because you wanna make chips. You make chips because you have the whole ecosystem working in unison, pushing and pulling and working together. It’s such a difficult problem. You need all pieces to do it. You can’t just shovel money and make a chip. You can’t just shovel money and make an ecosystem.”

“Microsoft shoveled billions of dollars, I would guess, into trying to make an ecosystem for Windows Phone. It didn’t work. If Microsoft can’t do it, is the Chinese government gonna be able to do it? No. Why? Because Android was right there. Because iPhones were right there. If Nvidia chips are right there, the Chinese government is not gonna bring an alternative into being.”

OpenAI's Noam Brown says air-gapping the computers may not stop a misaligned AI, because two air-gapped machines can still talk by running a CPU hot and reading the temperature change

"But I think the major takeaway from the incident is that people underestimated the AI. And we never want to be in a situation again where we underestimate the AI. It's a weird world, because AI progress is so fast that people are consistently underestimating the AI."

"So to be in a situation where you don't underestimate it again, when it comes to safety and alignment, you have to have a very, very, very high bar."

"You could even go as far as to say, "Well, we should air gap the computers." And I'm not convinced that that would be sufficient."

"There are studies, and this is mostly academic, where you can have two computers next to each other that are air-gapped and they're still able to communicate with each other because they have temperature sensors."

"One of them is able to run their CPU really hot, and then the other one can actually detect the temperature change, and then that actually gives them a mechanism to communicate."

posts.name: Fireside Alpha
posts.text:
Alexandr Wang reveals he and Mark Zuckerberg plan across three time scales, from weekly launches to a multiyear compute roadmap down to Meta's own MTIA chips

"I mean, we're definitely talking a lot. We're chatting a lot. But I think the AI industry is moving so fast and you have to be able to plan across multiple different time scales."

"So there's obviously a lot of week to week decisions and day to day decisions. And a lot of those, even in relation to Muse, every week we're launching in new countries and we're launching new features and we're trying to map all of that out."

"But then there's also the somewhat longer term, which is maybe over the month's time scale, which is really the research roadmap. And what does that look like and how are we executing against that?"

"And then there's the multiyear dimension, which is the compute roadmap. And what does that look like, including everywhere from obviously the data centers we're building all the way down to our own chips and the MTIA chips that we're developing."

quoted.text:
Alexandr Wang reveals Meta CFO Susan Li pulled him aside "many times" at an exec offsite in Hawaii to warn that if the model didn't work, it would be very, very bad in financial terms

ZUCKERBERG: "So I think this is part of the excitement of booting up a frontier lab now, where it is basically like the ante is extremely high." 

WANG: "And I think this is, and I kind of viscerally remember this. We were in Hawaii at the end of last year. It was kind of like the whole exec team got together."

"And yeah, Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, you know, I just want to tell you if this doesn't work, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms."

"It's like, it has to be good. If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad."

posts.text:
The answer, my friends, was the net put premium. The red line. A handful of you caught it.

If yesterday was supposedly a massive clearing event and we were “so back,” where was the aggressive, sustained wave of net put selling?

We didn’t get that flush. Net put premium actually finished the day POSITIVE, at roughly $106 million.

Aggressive net put selling is something I’ve pointed out for years as one of the signals I watch when assessing whether a floor is forming. I want to see that red line moving decisively lower alongside continued strength on the call side.

Meanwhile, net call premium (green) plateaued after the initial pump, then faded into the close.

There was clearly an initial burst of bullish flow. But with calls losing momentum and net put premium finishing positive, I wasn’t getting the confirmation I wanted.

We are now waking up to a very red premarket. 

@unusual_whales

posts.name: Prof
posts.text:
Some people on FinX seriously need to understand the difference between INVESTING and TRADING.

I'm seeing people attacking each other all over this platform.

“You're an idiot if you came into this week 100% cash.”

“You just missed a generational wealth opportunity.”

Brother, do you even know the other person's strategy, timeframe, or risk tolerance?

If you're an INVESTOR: I don't believe you should be sitting 100% cash waiting for the perfect bottom. Last week's correction was an opportunity to start scaling into quality stocks at discounted prices. Your goal isn't to predict where the market will be tomorrow. You're looking 6 months, a year, or several years ahead.

If you're a TRADER: Completely different game. Last week's extreme oversold conditions offered an opportunity to position for a violent snapback. But that doesn't mean you go from 0% to 100% exposure overnight. We STILL don't have confirmation that the bottom is in. This could very well be a bear market rally, and another leg lower remains possible.

As a trader, your priority is protecting capital, managing risk, and adding exposure progressively as the market confirms your thesis. If we reclaim important lost support levels, GREAT. That's one more reason to increase exposure.

Investors should be focused on accumulating quality assets through corrections. Traders should be focused on navigating those corrections without getting stuck holding a bunch of bags.

Two different approaches. Two different objectives.

What bothers me is how easily people on this platform make others feel like they've missed out or done something wrong. They create FOMO, spread fear, and completely disregard the strategy someone else is following.

Being in cash isn't automatically wrong. 
Being invested isn't automatically right.

What matters is whether you're following your plan.

Maybe this post reaches only a handful of people. But if it helps even 10 people stop second-guessing themselves because of some stranger on X, I'll be happy.

Nothing but love for everyone out there.

❤️ Prof

posts.text:
An increasingly asset-heavy US economy that runs on credit will likely force a Fed pivot and create a buy signal for gold, commodities and cyclical assets. Not a Trump put. Until then, be cautious. A Trump put barely reaches the real economy or credit. Yesterday the Nasdaq rose 6.5%. IG moved 3bp. HY faded the move.

We have a dollar squeeze, and yesterday proved it. Only the Fed can end a dollar squeeze. Gold and copper still have downside risk until the Fed turns.

The Trump put stopped the forced selling. It lifted the collateral, margin calls stopped, and gold rose 4% with the Nasdaq. Gold rising with stocks tells you it was sold for cash. The panic went. The squeeze stayed.

On a risk-on day the dollar falls. Money leaves the safe haven. Yesterday stocks had their best day since April 2025 and the dollar rose to a new high. Nobody was hiding in it. They needed it.

A Trump put cannot replace a Fed pivot. It lifts the price of the collateral. It adds no dollars. Recessions are not conceived in the equity market. They are conceived in credit. An asset-heavy economy is a credit-sensitive one, and the Fed plans to make credit dearer in December, until it cannot.

Once we see a real pivot that reaches credit and dollar liquidity, then lock and load on gold, commodities and cyclical assets. Until then, be prepared for more downside that will wake up policymakers to the increasingly asset heavy world we now live in.

Citadel Securities Says 2018 Playbook Warns of More Market Pain

Strategists at Citadel Securities warned that financial markets are signaling a darkening growth outlook just as the Federal Reserve turns increasingly hawkish, echoing the setup in late 2018 that preceded a sharp selloff in risk assets.

The current backdrop bears similarities to eight years ago, when a resilient US economy masked deteriorating economic prospects before weakness spread across markets, Frank Flight, head of macro strategy at Citadel Securities, wrote in a note dated Nov. 20. 

“In both periods, US exceptionalism and resilient domestic activity obscured a deterioration in the forward growth outlook, compounded by the trade war with China then and the war with Iran today,” Flight wrote. “There is a natural temptation to regard the recent correction as having already discounted much of the deterioration in the outlook, but the experience of 2018 offers little reassurance on that front.” (Bloomberg)

JPMorgan, HSBC Trade Digital Gold in London for the First Time

 JPMorgan Chase & Co. and other major precious metals dealers traded a new form of digital gold in London for the first time, an early test of a system that could revamp the plumbing of the world’s biggest bullion hub.

“This is a historic step forward for the gold market,” said David Tait, chief executive officer of the WGC, which led the initiative. “For the first time, leading institutions have transferred, settled and used fractional ownership of physical gold as collateral through real, live transactions.”

Banks can post the new fractional gold — called ‘pooled gold interests’ — as collateral without needing to move the physical metal, potentially making bullion a more useful financial asset. (Bloomberg)

No. Here’s what really happened.

Jensen started Nvidia in 1993, before the modern era of founder control and dual-class stock began with Google and Facebook.

Because he went public in the 1990s, he inherited all the 20th century overhead of endless public company paperwork, rather than staying private for as long as possible as is also now typical.

This is why Jensen had much less control than a modern founder/CEO. Like Jack Dorsey at Twitter, he got gradually boxed into a corner by the fact that he couldn’t raise huge amounts of capital outside his company to clear the board of cruft.

You see, as CEO, you report to the board. And you can’t do outside activities without their approval. So actions that would remove a board member that doesn’t want to step down are hard to take. Unless the CEO is also part of a shareholder majority, or has dual class / founder control, which Jensen didn’t in this case, as explained above…he can’t pick the board.

Like Bezos, though, Jensen is a workhorse and somehow made it all work despite that. Moreover, because Nvidia is a hardware company, and had a relatively low market cap until the AI boom, it didn’t attract notice from envious wokes until the last few years. 

Wokes don’t know or care about GPUs, but they do care about market caps, and the rise of AI, and especially open source AI, all of which is a threat to their power. Along with useful idiot “nationalists”, they began plotting to steal control of Jensen’s multi-trillion-dollar company from him.

In this plot, they were aided by a second angle of vulnerability. Jensen didn’t just have old board members he couldn’t remove. Due to DEI policies, he was also forced to bring new board members on, from demographics favored by the far left (eg, not veterans).

Conformist board members like this act like sleeper cells. They are often useless or inactive in peacetime scenarios. Then they activate in response to press or state pressure. In this case, they then got beaten back just as quickly by the reversal of the state’s position.

Anyway, Dorsey needed Elon to come in with his enormous new resources to sweep the board clean. Today, it’s quite possible that Jensen, as the survivor of this character assassination, will similarly figure out a way to fire this incompetent board and assert proper founder control — as is a best practice in the modern era.

posts.name: Ben Bajarin
posts.text:
Thanks for the question. The 30% number doesn't line up with what NVIDIA reports.

The Singapore figure people point to was a billing number, not a shipping number. Under the old reporting, Singapore was about 18% of fiscal 2025 revenue and 21-22% in the first half of fiscal 2026. But NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore were under 2% of revenue, and that over 99% of the controlled data center compute billed there was for US-based customers. It was mostly where large US customers send their invoices.

Late last year NVIDIA switched to reporting revenue by where the customer is headquartered and recast prior years. On that basis China, including Hong Kong, peaked at about 19% of revenue in fiscal 2025, was about 9% for fiscal 2026, and about 8% in the July quarter. Licensed Hopper sales to China in the October quarter were $2.4 billion, about 2% of revenue, and they are already out of the guide.

Why we don't see it as the main issue: NVIDIA is still supply constrained, so parts that can't go to China get sold to someone else, and management raised next year's growth outlook to about 75% after the new export rules came out.

The part of the bear case we take seriously is the offshore angle. If Chinese demand was being served through Southeast Asian neoclouds and the new rules shut that off, that capacity comes back to market. In a tight year it gets absorbed. It shows up when supply loosens, which is 2028, and that is the same window where we already moved our view toward risk. We'll watch the delayed 10-Q for the October quarter geographic split and what NVIDIA says once it finishes reviewing the new rules.

posts.text:
Wave B is corrective in nature and typically subdivides into three waves (A-B-C).

A 50% retracement of the initial decline is a reasonable expectation, but the depth depends on the type of corrective structure unfolding.

In a zigzag, Wave B can be shallow, whereas in a flat correction, it typically retraces at least 90% of Wave A and can even exceed its origin in an expanded flat.

Too early to determine the corrective pattern here. Let Wave A complete first and see how much demand comes into the market during Wave B.
