posts.text:
Founders produce higher returns than non-founders. This is an empirical fact.

So: business school curricula should be changed, and good governance should be redefined as founder control and dual-class stock. Shareholders are still protected by easy liquidation and their ability to fund new entrants. After all, you don’t invest in a company based on who’s on the board. That’s largely ceremonial.

The key difference from the 20th century is that it was prohibitively difficult in 1950 to found a manufacturing company, because assembly lines cost so much, the communists controlled much of the world, and even America had 90% marginal tax rates. It was the century of centralization, the individual powerless before the institution.

Today it is no longer prohibitively difficult to found a tech company, because software costs so little, much of the world has turned to free markets, and capital flows at the speed of the Internet. This is the century of decentralization, at least in the West, with the institution falling to the individual.

For example: Anthropic was started just a few years ago and is beating even Google at its own game. If we get many open weights models, their moat will also in turn erode.

So: all 20th century corporate governance was based on the idea that “the company is hard to replace, but its CEO isn’t.” The Harvard MBA is premised on the professional manager. It was expensive to start a new company with all the assembly lines, so make sure it doesn’t fail by making every employee replaceable. Managers were abundant so capital became the scarce asset.

By contrast, the entire 21st century model is based on the idea that “A tech founder is hard to replace, but the company isn’t.” The YCombinator model is premised on the startup founder. It is inexpensive to start a new company with a few lines of code, so make sure it doesn’t fail by having an irreplaceable team. Capital is abundant so founders become the scarce asset.

quoted.text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

posts.name: James Seyffart
posts.text:
There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
From The Dotcom Bust To The AI Boom History Warns Of A Growing Credit Risk

The hyperscaler credit default swap basket reached 115.6 on November 24, rising approximately 12% from its November lows and reaching a new high within the displayed period.

This is particularly concerning because skepticism surrounding AI is increasingly spreading beyond equity valuations into corporate credit markets, where investors are reassessing financial sustainability and demanding greater compensation for credit risk.

Yesterday’s extraordinary equity rally following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement restored some investor confidence. It did not resolve the underlying financing vulnerabilities.

Historical Precedent

During the telecommunications boom of the late 1990s, companies committed enormous amounts of capital toward infrastructure based on expectations of explosive future internet demand.

Technology credit spreads began widening in early 2000 before the broader investment cycle collapsed. Financing became increasingly restrictive, capital expenditure contracted and bankruptcies followed.

The internet ultimately revolutionized the global economy. That did not prevent enormous financial losses among the institutions financing its initial expansion.

Similarly, during 2007, financial sector credit spreads began deteriorating before the full extent of the economic contraction became apparent.

Today, AI may represent another transformative technological advancement accompanied by an unsustainable investment cycle.

The Growing Financing Problem

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr recently identified several vulnerabilities within the AI financing ecosystem.

•  More than $800 billion in projected corporate debt among seven major AI companies by year end

•  More than $3 trillion in potential contractual and other financial obligations

•  More than $100 billion in cumulative equity investments by hyperscalers and GPU producers in AI laboratories and cloud startups

These exposures are not equivalent to outstanding debt and should not be added together. Nevertheless, they reveal considerable financial interconnectedness.

Companies are increasingly financing customers that purchase their infrastructure, creating demand that may depend heavily on continued access to external capital rather than independently generated revenue.

Meanwhile, long duration debt is financing equipment that faces rapid technological depreciation and potential obsolescence.

The Macroeconomic Transmission

AI investment has become an important source of economic growth, supporting semiconductor manufacturing, construction, electrical infrastructure, utilities, logistics and professional services.

These industries appear independently throughout economic statistics, yet portions of their demand originate from the same investment cycle.

Persistent credit spread widening could increase borrowing costs, undermine investment returns, delay infrastructure projects and eventually force capital expenditure reductions and workforce restructuring.

This is developing while household delinquency is rising, small business bankruptcies are accelerating, commercial real estate remains distressed and labor market hiring is historically subdued.

Unlike previous investment busts, persistent energy inflation is also limiting the Federal Reserve’s ability to provide monetary relief.

The greatest concern is that financial market deleveraging is beginning to threaten one of the principal investment cycles sustaining aggregate economic growth.

Widening hyperscaler CDS spreads do not establish an imminent credit crisis. However, historical precedent demonstrates why the transition from deteriorating equity valuations to deteriorating credit conditions deserves considerably greater attention.

The equity market can celebrate technological potential. The credit market must ultimately determine whether the financial obligations incurred to realize that potential can be serviced.

posts.text:
JUST IN: Attorney General Todd Blanche says the national-security call on Jensen Huang was a collective consensus across agencies, and that he has no information on Huang's clearance status

Q: "How did the administration, though, just setting aside the potential criminal investigations, actually make a determination that there was no national security risk related to Jensen Huang? And who, is it DOJ, is it the Pentagon, is assessing Huang's continuing access to sensitive national security information?"

BLANCHE: "How we make that type of determination is, there's a whole bunch of ways we do it. We use the intelligence community, the FBI, the information we know. We talk to witnesses. I mean, that's something that we do."

"I know there's heightened focus on this situation, but that's something that the law enforcement partners and that the leadership in this country, whether it's commerce or treasury, state department, the attorney general, me, it's a collective consensus that we reach all the time in all kinds of different cases, not just in this case."

"And how we determine whether a private citizen has access to information, I mean, there's clearances, there's background clearances, there's information that, depending on the project or the job, they're allowed to have or not allowed to have. So it depends on the issue specifically."

"I don't have any information about even what his clearance status is. But I don't know. I mean, I don't want you to take that as an indication that he is or is not keeping his clearance. I just have no information about that."

quoted.text:
JUST IN: Attorney General Todd Blanche says that if the DOJ had information Jensen Huang was committing crimes, "I would have certainly told the President"

"Well, so, no, what the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him."

"And so I'm not going to get into communications I have with the President about it, but what he was saying was true, right?"

"So what he was saying is exactly right, which is that to the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that's something that I would have certainly told the President had it been true."

posts.name: Peter Schiff
posts.text:
OCIF, the agency created by the Puerto Rico government to oversee banks, appointed a trustee with zero prior banking experience to liquidate my completely solvent bank. What made his job simple was that the bank had no loans on its books and no debt on its balance sheet. 3,370 customers held deposits of just under $67 million consisting of cash, precious metals, and mutual funds, which have since appreciated to over $100 million. The bank had more than enough liquidity to pay every customer in full, with funds left over for me.

Yet after nearly four years and five months, the Trustee will have paid himself more than $1 million to return just $4.7 million to a mere 63 customers, out of the 679 claims the Trustee acknowledges having received. That's less than 10% of claims, representing fewer than 3% of customers being paid less than 5% of deposits.

That amounts to almost $17,000 per claim, or almost 23% of the value of paid claims. His quarterly payments have been increasing over time, with the most recent haul netting him $205,540. At this rate, he is now "earning" $822,160 per year. Worse, there is no end in sight to the escalation. My guess is that over the next full year, he will clear over $1 million.

This is why he has no incentive to pay claims and every incentive to keep the gravy train running as long as possible. Plus, mine is not the only bank he is liquidating, nor is it the only work he is doing. My guess is that this is just a side hustle that nets him many times what he could possibly earn working full-time in a truly private-sector job.

Worse, this is not how much the Trustee has spent liquidating my bank, just what he has paid himself to do it. In total, the Trustee has spent $2.6 million. That's almost $41,300 per paid claim, or 55% of the total value of claims paid.

What makes this so frustrating is that none of this was necessary. The OCIF Commissioner sacrificed thousands of innocent customers purely as a publicity stunt. She lied that the action was meant to protect customers, but the facts show that customers were in no danger at all until the Puerto Rico government stepped in to "protect" them.

posts.name: Nezih Gökay
posts.text:
1936’da Japonya’nın Hyogo bölgesinde, fakir bir çiftçi ailesinin en küçük çocuğu olarak doğan bir adam, 19 yaşında pet shop’ta çalışırken borsaya başlıyor. 

Bugün 88 yaşında, hala her gün işlem yapıyor ve yaklaşık 2 milyar yenlik (14 milyon dolar civarı) bir servete sahip.

Adamın adı Shigeru Fujimoto. Kobe’de yaşıyor. Lise bittikten sonra bir pet shop’ta işe giriyor. Dükkâna sık gelen bir aracı kurum yöneticisiyle sohbet ediyor, adam ona hisse almasını tavsiye ediyor. Fujimoto ilk hisselerini o dönemde alıyor. Sharp ve petrol şirketi Eneos gibi isimler.

Sonra kendi pet shop’unu açıyor, ardından mahjong salonu işletiyor. 1986’da salonları satıp 65 milyon yen elde ediyor ve tam zamanlı yatırımcı oluyor. O yıllar Japonya’nın balon dönemi. Varlıkları 1 milyar yene çıkıyor.

Balon patlıyor. Serveti 200 milyon yene düşüyor. 1995’te Kobe depremi geliyor. Apartmanının girişi yıkılıyor, tanıştığı birini kaybediyor. Ama devam ediyor.

2002’de, 66 yaşındayken bilgisayar alıyor ve internet üzerinden işlem yapmaya başlıyor. Bugün odasında üç monitör var. Sabah erken kalkıyor, ABD piyasasını takip ediyor, günde yüzlerce emir giriyor. Bazen sabah 2’de uyanıyor.

Geçen yıl bir şirkette yüzde 5’ten fazla hisse aldığı ortaya çıkınca o hisse yüzde 17 artıyor. Yerel medya ona “Japonya’nın Warren Buffett’ı” diyor. Kendisi hâlâ araba ve cep telefonu kullanmıyor. Para biriktirmenin eğlenceli olduğunu söylüyor.

Düşünün, adam pet shop’ta çalışırken başlamış. Aslında o dönemde 19 yaşında, çiftçi çocuğu, ne anlar? diye düşünenler olmuştur. Ama 70 yıla yakın devam etmiş.

Normalde insan bu kadar uzun süre aktif işlem yapan birinin büyük servet biriktirdiğini beklemiyor. Yani sıradan bir dükkan çalışanı olarak başlamış, deprem ve balon patlamasını atlatmış.

Adam o yıllarda gördüğü fırsatı ve sonra da bilgisayarı değerlendirmiş. Nereden baksanız ilginç bir süreklilik.

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
Wereldkampioen sparen, verliezer in koopkracht

Nederlanders beleggen voor 242 miljard!

Dat is de laatste update van De Nederlandsche Bank. Liefst 242 miljard euro van het vrije vermogen (dus exclusief pensioenen en woningen) wordt belegd. Dat klinkt gigantisch, maar die kwalificatie verdient een flinke nuance.

Nederlanders hebben namelijk nog veel meer spaargeld. Met 660 miljard euro vertegenwoordigen spaarrekeningen een duizelingwekkende 73% van ons vermogen. Aandelen zijn goed voor 19% en obligaties voor 8%.

Die enorme berg spaargeld is bepaald geen goede keuze geweest. De rente is immers structureel te laag, waardoor inflatie de koopkracht van je spaargeld opeet. En niet zo’n beetje ook: over de afgelopen vijf jaar is 17% aan koopkracht verdampt. Met spaargeld op de rekening in 2021 kun je nu bijna een vijfde minder boodschappen doen.

Stel dat de verdeling van het vermogen van Nederlandse huishoudens constant was gebleven. Geen vreemde aanname, want Nederlanders maken al tientallen jaren een sport van sparen. Dan was de koopkracht van het Nederlandse vermogen met 7% gedaald. Een fors verlies dus.

Had je dat spaargeld in aandelen gestopt, dan was je koopkracht met 26% toegenomen. Je had dan wel meer risico genomen, daar moet je rekening mee houden, maar je had in ieder geval geen koopkracht verloren.

Was je zo slim geweest om, zoals wij voorstellen, ook een deel van je geld in goud te beleggen, dan was je nog beter af geweest. Goud leverde, zelfs na de prijsdaling van de afgelopen maanden, over de afgelopen vijf jaar een rendement van 99% op, en dat is dus ook na aftrek van inflatie.

Een portefeuille van 60% aandelen, 20% goud en 20% spaargeld had de koopkracht van Nederlanders gemiddeld 42% vooruitgeholpen. Vergelijk dat met de werkelijke mix en je houdt een koopkrachtverschil van bijna 50 procentpunten over. Stel je eens voor wat je daarmee had kunnen doen.
Is sparen wel veilig? Niet als je meetelt wat bepalend is voor je echte resultaat: inflatie.

Nog niet aan het beleggen?

De dalende koersen van de afgelopen weken hebben je alvast geholpen aan een beter instapmoment.

posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
When I post about France heading toward a debt crisis, someone always replies, "But look at the US debt." Guess what, France and the United States carry comparable public debt burdens, roughly 119% of GDP for France and 127% for the US, yet the nature of that debt differs sharply.

US Treasuries sit at the center of the global financial system. They are the deepest, most liquid safe asset, the primary reserve-currency instrument, and the preferred high-quality collateral. Central banks, money-market funds, insurers, and institutional investors hold them not merely by choice but as a structural necessity for liquidity, risk management, and reserves. Flight-to-safety demand reinforces this role in stress. That captive, recurring demand gives the United States a wide margin for error.

French government bonds enjoy no such privilege. Non-residents hold a large share (around 50–60%), but this is discretionary demand driven by yield, index inclusion, and relative value within the euro area. French banks and insurers hold some for regulatory or portfolio reasons, yet nothing forces global investors to own French bonds the way the system forces them to own US Treasuries. When political or fiscal risks rise, that capital can leave quickly.

This distinction matters because France has shown little to none willingness to address the underlying drivers of its debt path. Successive governments have struggled with pension costs, and the two presidential candidates currently leading most polls, Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, both campaign on reversing the recent rise in the retirement age and returning it toward 60–62.

Markets have so far more or less tolerated this, helped by the European Central Bank’s residual presence, but tolerance is not structural. Unlike the United States, France cannot rely on a permanent global bid for its paper. If deficits remain elevated and reform stalls, spreads will eventually widen even further, funding costs will rise, and the adjustment will be imposed from outside, through higher borrowing rates, forced spending restraint, or both, rather than chosen at home. 

The arithmetic is not especially subtle, only the timing is uncertain. The second Euro crisis will begin in France, and it will take down the entire Eurozone with it. Prove me wrong if you can. https://x.com/michaelaarouet/status/2117895061711077714/photo/1
